reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: X-linked recessive disorder caused by variants in TAZ (also called TAFAZZIN), encoding the enzyme tafazzin, so it almost exclusively affects males
Tafazzin remodels cardiolipin, the signature phospholipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane, so its deficiency impairs mitochondrial structure and oxidative phosphorylation
The core clinical triad is cardiomyopathy (often dilated, sometimes with left ventricular non-compaction), skeletal myopathy with proximal weakness, and cyclical or persistent neutropenia
Growth delay is common in childhood, sometimes with a characteristic catch-up growth in later adolescence
Recurrent bacterial infections result from the neutropenia and can be life-threatening
A useful biochemical clue is raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid (a form of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria) and an abnormal monolysocardiolipin-to-cardiolipin ratio
Cardiomyopathy may present in utero, in infancy or later, and can fluctuate in severity
Diagnosis is confirmed by cardiolipin analysis and TAZ genetic testing; management is supportive with attention to cardiac failure and infection risk
reference.pathophysiology: Barth syndrome is caused by deficiency of tafazzin, a transacylase that remodels immature cardiolipin into its mature form containing predominantly unsaturated fatty acyl chains. Mature cardiolipin is concentrated in the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it stabilises the respiratory chain complexes and supports oxidative phosphorylation, membrane curvature and cristae structure. Loss of tafazzin leaves an abnormal cardiolipin profile with accumulation of the intermediate monolysocardiolipin, destabilising the respiratory chain and impairing energy production. Tissues with high energy demand, particularly cardiac and skeletal muscle, are most affected, and mitochondrial dysfunction in the bone marrow contributes to the neutropenia. The disturbed leucine and mitochondrial metabolism underlies the 3-methylglutaconic aciduria.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic dilated cardiomyopathies and left ventricular non-compaction
Primary mitochondrial cardiomyopathies and other causes of 3-methylglutaconic aciduria
Congenital or cyclical neutropenia of other causes
Glycogen storage disease with cardiac involvement (for example Pompe disease)
additionalInvestigations: Cardiolipin analysis with the monolysocardiolipin-to-cardiolipin ratio in blood spots or tissue
Urine organic acids showing raised 3-methylglutaconic acid
Serial full blood counts to characterise cyclical or persistent neutropenia
Echocardiography and cardiac assessment for cardiomyopathy and non-compaction
Creatine kinase and assessment of skeletal muscle function
redFlags: Heart failure from dilated cardiomyopathy in an infant or child
Serious or recurrent bacterial infection during neutropenic episodes
Ventricular arrhythmia or sudden deterioration in cardiac function
Severe hypotonia and weakness impairing feeding or breathing
reference.prognosis: Historically Barth syndrome carried high early mortality from heart failure and infection, but with modern cardiac care, monitoring and management of neutropenia many patients now survive into adulthood. Prognosis depends largely on the severity and course of the cardiomyopathy and on preventing serious infections.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy with dilated cardiomyopathy by not checking for neutropenia or 3-methylglutaconic aciduria
Attributing recurrent infections to an unrelated immune problem
Assuming the cardiomyopathy is static, when it can fluctuate and worsen
Missing the raised urinary 3-methylglutaconic acid as a diagnostic clue
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Standard heart-failure therapy with agents such as ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and diuretics for the dilated cardiomyopathy
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor to correct neutropenia, with prompt antibiotic treatment of intercurrent bacterial infection
Consideration of antibiotic prophylaxis given the risk of recurrent life-threatening sepsis
Nutritional support and physiotherapy for skeletal myopathy and growth delay
Regular echocardiographic and cardiac rhythm surveillance for progression, left ventricular non-compaction and arrhythmia
Consideration of cardiac transplantation for refractory end-stage heart failure
Multidisciplinary care spanning cardiology, haematology, metabolic medicine and dietetics
Genetic counselling for X-linked inheritance, with carrier testing of female relatives and family screening
